Narrative 08/23/2022 7:22 PM PDT 68 years old Female, smoker with recent onset of short distance right leg claudication ** TECHNIQUE **: PROCEDURE SUMMARY: - Arterial access with ultrasound guidance -Right lower extremity angiography as described below - Arterial interventions as described below - Post intervention Right lower extremity angiography Medications: Please see nursing record for sedation medications used. Other intraprocedural medications: None Radiation Dose -please see nursing records for radiation dose. Contrast: Please see nursing record for contrast dose. ** FINDINGS **: PROCEDURE DETAILS: Informed consent for the procedure including risks, benefits and alternatives was obtained and time-out was performed prior to the procedure.  The right-sided access site was prepared and draped using maximal sterile barrier technique including cutaneous antisepsis. Local analgesia was achieved with 2% lidocaine administered subcutaneously. The left common femoral artery was accessed with standard micropuncture technique and a sheath was placed.  Omniflush catheter was advanced into the distal abdominal aorta and pelvic angiogram was performed. Over angled glide wire, omniflush catheter was advanced into the right common femoral artery and the lower extremity runoff was performed to the right foot. Findings: Severe diffuse atheromatous changes are seen throughout the visualized arterial structures. Extensive calcifications are noted. The vessels as a whole are also quite gracile, especially of the iliac arteries bilaterally. Both internal iliac arteries are diseased but patent. The right common femoral artery is patent without significant stenosis. The right profunda is disease but is hypertrophied. There is diffuse disease in the SFA with short segment of occlusion in the abductor canal. There is a second longer occlusive segment at distal SFA and a third moderate to high-grade segmental stenosis at the junction of the distal SFA and popliteal arteries. There is two-vessel runoff in the leg with the peroneal artery being the dominant vessel. Anterior tibial is also patent. There is patency of the dorsal pedis as well as the distal posterior tibial artery plantar arteries are patent. Interventional procedure: A total of 6000 units of heparin were used for the procedure. In addition 400 mcg of intra-arterial nitroglycerin also were used. A 6 French destination sheath was advanced over wire so that the distal tip was within the lower right external iliac artery. An 0.035 advantage wire with crossing catheter was used to successfully traverse the occluded segments. Then, a 6 mm spider distal protection device was deployed in the distal popliteal artery. Then, a medium Hawk 1 directional atherectomy device was used to atherectomized all of the mentioned lesions. Approximately 4 passes were made in each segment. Then 5 mm chocolate balloon was used to dilate all of the affected segments. This was followed up with the use of 5 mm DCB over the treated segments. Follow-up arteriogram showed excellent angiographic results with complete patency of the SFA established. The spider distal protection device was retrieved. Post intervention: Right lower extremity runoff was performed to the foot. There is no evidence for embolic phenomena. Physical examination revealed a palpable right dorsal pedis artery, whereas prior to the procedure there was none. Vascular sheath was removed and hemostasis achieved with minx closure device. Complications: No immediate complications. ** HISTORY **: 68 years old Female, smoker with recent onset of short distance right leg claudication ** TECHNIQUE **: PROCEDURE SUMMARY: - Arterial access with ultrasound guidance -Right lower extremity angiography as described below - Arterial interventions as described below - Post intervention Right lower extremity angiography Medications: Please see nursing record for sedation medications used. Other intraprocedural medications: None Radiation Dose -please see nursing records for radiation dose. Contrast: Please see nursing record for contrast dose. ** FINDINGS **: PROCEDURE DETAILS: Informed consent for the procedure including risks, benefits and alternatives was obtained and time-out was performed prior to the procedure. The right-sided access site was prepared and draped using maximal sterile barrier technique including cutaneous antisepsis. Local analgesia was achieved with 2% lidocaine administered subcutaneously. The left common femoral artery was accessed with standard micropuncture technique and a sheath was placed. Omniflush catheter was advanced into the distal abdominal aorta and pelvic angiogram was performed. Over angled glide wire, omniflush catheter was advanced into the right common femoral artery and the lower extremity runoff was performed to the right foot. Findings: Severe diffuse atheromatous changes are seen throughout the visualized arterial structures. Extensive calcifications are noted. The vessels as a whole are also quite gracile, especially of the iliac arteries bilaterally. Both internal iliac arteries are diseased but patent. The right common femoral artery is patent without significant stenosis. The right profunda is disease but is hypertrophied. There is diffuse disease in the SFA with short segment of occlusion in the abductor canal. There is a second longer occlusive segment at distal SFA and a third moderate to high-grade segmental stenosis at the junction of the distal SFA and popliteal arteries. There is two-vessel runoff in the leg with the peroneal artery being the dominant vessel. Anterior tibial is also patent. There is patency of the dorsal pedis as well as the distal posterior tibial artery plantar arteries are patent. Interventional procedure: A total of 6000 units of heparin were used for the procedure. In addition 400 mcg of intra-arterial nitroglycerin also were used. A 6 French destination sheath was advanced over wire so that the distal tip was within the lower right external iliac artery. An 0.035 advantage wire with crossing catheter was used to successfully traverse the occluded segments. Then, a 6 mm spider distal protection device was deployed in the distal popliteal artery. Then, a medium Hawk 1 directional atherectomy device was used to atherectomized all of the mentioned lesions. Approximately 4 passes were made in each segment. Then 5 mm chocolate balloon was used to dilate all of the affected segments. This was followed up with the use of 5 mm DCB over the treated segments. Follow-up arteriogram showed excellent angiographic results with complete patency of the SFA established. The spider distal protection device was retrieved. Post intervention: Right lower extremity runoff was performed to the foot. There is no evidence for embolic phenomena. ** IMPRESSION **: Angiography of the pelvis and right leg demonstrates multifocal occlusions and stenoses of the superficial femoral artery. This was successfully treated with directional atherectomy and drug coated balloon angioplasty with excellent angiographic and clinical result. The patient was loaded with Plavix. She is to maintain Plavix treatment for at least 3 months. TPMG Chiefs of Emergency Medicine have endorsed the recommendations from the American College of Physicians and the American College of Cardiology: when D-dimer testing is applied in the evaluation of pulmonary embolism in patients without a high pre-test probability and in whom acute PE cannot be excluded using the PE Rule-Out Criteria (PERC), then age-adjusted D-dimer thresholds (age x 0.01 ug/mL FEU) should be used in patients over 50 years old instead of the 0.50 ug/mL FEU threshold to determine the medical necessity of imaging.

Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT):

D-dimer <0.50 ug/mL FEU in a patient with low pre-test probability makes a diagnosis of DVT very unlikely. However, a D-dimer >=0.50 ug/mL FEU is nonspecific and may require additional diagnostic testing.

Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC):

Use reference interval of <0.50 ug/mL FEU. TPMG Chiefs of Emergency Medicine have endorsed the recommendations from the American College of Physicians and the American College of Cardiology: when D-dimer testing is applied in the evaluation of pulmonary embolism in patients without a high pre-test probability and in whom acute PE cannot be excluded using the PE Rule-Out Criteria (PERC), then age-adjusted D-dimer thresholds (age x 0.01 ug/mL FEU) should be used in patients over 50 years old instead of the 0.50 ug/mL FEU threshold to determine the medical necessity of imaging.

Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT):

D-dimer <0.50 ug/mL FEU in a patient with low pre-test probability makes a diagnosis of DVT very unlikely. However, a D-dimer >=0.50 ug/mL FEU is nonspecific and may require additional diagnostic testing.

Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC):

Use reference interval of <0.50 ug/mL FEU. Narrative 01/05/2018 4:12 PM PST 63 year old woman with weight loss and abdominal pain. ** FINDINGS **: Technique:  Multiple contiguous axial CT images were obtained through the abdomen and pelvis following the administration of 106 mL of Omnipaque-300 intravenous contrast media. Positive oral contrast was not administered. Multiplanar reformats were obtained. CTDI: 6.31 mGy DLP: 278.41 mGy-cm Phantom: Body 32 Comparison: None CT Abdomen: Lung Base: Mild patchy consolidative and groundglass opacity at the extreme right lung base. Centrilobular emphysematous changes are noted at the lung bases. No pleural or pericardial effusion. Liver, Gallbladder, and Biliary System: The liver is normal in size and contour, without focal lesions. The gallbladder appears unremarkable. There is no intra-or extrahepatic biliary ductal dilatation. Spleen: The spleen is normal in size and no focal splenic lesions are seen. Pancreas: No concerning pancreatic lesions or pancreatic ductal dilatation are seen. Kidneys and Ureters: No concerning renal mass or hydronephrosis bilaterally. Some prominence of an extrarenal pelvis bilaterally, likely incidental. There there are multiple areas of left renal cortical thickening, likely chronic sequela of prior nonspecific insult. Adrenals: Unremarkable. Bowel: Overall, evaluation of bowel is limited by scant intra-abdominal fat. The stomach is decompressed and unremarkable. Abdominal small bowel loops are nondilated and without evidence for obstruction. The appendix is not identified in the right lower quadrant, no abnormal appendix is not seen. Intra-abdominal colon appears unremarkable. Lymph Nodes: Scattered mesenteric and retroperitoneal lymph nodes are identified, none of which appear pathologically enlarged. Vasculature: Atherosclerotic calcifications involve the abdominal aorta and branches. The aorta is of normal caliber. The portal venous system is patent. Peritoneum: No free fluid or free air. CT Pelvis: Bowel loops: Intrapelvic loop of small bowel appear unremarkable, without dilatation or wall thickening. The sigmoid colon and rectum appear unremarkable. A mild pericolonic edema of the descending and sigmoid colon is equivocal. Bladder: Unremarkable. Pelvic organs: Unremarkable. No free fluid is seen. Lymph Nodes: No pathologically enlarged pelvic lymph nodes are seen. Soft Tissues and Bones: No concerning abnormalities. Narrative 08/23/2022 7:22 PM PDT 68 years old Female, smoker with recent onset of short distance right leg claudication ** TECHNIQUE **: PROCEDURE SUMMARY: - Arterial access with ultrasound guidance -Right lower extremity angiography as described below - Arterial interventions as described below - Post intervention Right lower extremity angiography Medications: Please see nursing record for sedation medications used. Other intraprocedural medications: None Radiation Dose -please see nursing records for radiation dose. Contrast: Please see nursing record for contrast dose. ** FINDINGS **: PROCEDURE DETAILS: Informed consent for the procedure including risks, benefits and alternatives was obtained and time-out was performed prior to the procedure.  The right-sided access site was prepared and draped using maximal sterile barrier technique including cutaneous antisepsis. Local analgesia was achieved with 2% lidocaine administered subcutaneously. The left common femoral artery was accessed with standard micropuncture technique and a sheath was placed.  Omniflush catheter was advanced into the distal abdominal aorta and pelvic angiogram was performed. Over angled glide wire, omniflush catheter was advanced into the right common femoral artery and the lower extremity runoff was performed to the right foot. Findings: Severe diffuse atheromatous changes are seen throughout the visualized arterial structures. Extensive calcifications are noted. The vessels as a whole are also quite gracile, especially of the iliac arteries bilaterally. Both internal iliac arteries are diseased but patent. The right common femoral artery is patent without significant stenosis. The right profunda is disease but is hypertrophied. There is diffuse disease in the SFA with short segment of occlusion in the abductor canal. There is a second longer occlusive segment at distal SFA and a third moderate to high-grade segmental stenosis at the junction of the distal SFA and popliteal arteries. There is two-vessel runoff in the leg with the peroneal artery being the dominant vessel. Anterior tibial is also patent. There is patency of the dorsal pedis as well as the distal posterior tibial artery plantar arteries are patent. Interventional procedure: A total of 6000 units of heparin were used for the procedure. In addition 400 mcg of intra-arterial nitroglycerin also were used. A 6 French destination sheath was advanced over wire so that the distal tip was within the lower right external iliac artery. An 0.035 advantage wire with crossing catheter was used to successfully traverse the occluded segments. Then, a 6 mm spider distal protection device was deployed in the distal popliteal artery. Then, a medium Hawk 1 directional atherectomy device was used to atherectomized all of the mentioned lesions. Approximately 4 passes were made in each segment. Then 5 mm chocolate balloon was used to dilate all of the affected segments. This was followed up with the use of 5 mm DCB over the treated segments. Follow-up arteriogram showed excellent angiographic results with complete patency of the SFA established. The spider distal protection device was retrieved. Post intervention: Right lower extremity runoff was performed to the foot. There is no evidence for embolic phenomena. Physical examination revealed a palpable right dorsal pedis artery, whereas prior to the procedure there was none. Vascular sheath was removed and hemostasis achieved with minx closure device. Complications: No immediate complications. ** HISTORY **: 68 years old Female, smoker with recent onset of short distance right leg claudication ** TECHNIQUE **: PROCEDURE SUMMARY: - Arterial access with ultrasound guidance -Right lower extremity angiography as described below - Arterial interventions as described below - Post intervention Right lower extremity angiography Medications: Please see nursing record for sedation medications used. TPMG Chiefs of Emergency Medicine have endorsed the recommendations from the American College of Physicians and the American College of Cardiology: when D-dimer testing is applied in the evaluation of pulmonary embolism in patients without a high pre-test probability and in whom acute PE cannot be excluded using the PE Rule-Out Criteria (PERC), then age-adjusted D-dimer thresholds (age x 0.01 ug/mL FEU) should be used in patients over 50 years old instead of the 0.50 ug/mL FEU threshold to determine the medical necessity of imaging.

Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT):

D-dimer <0.50 ug/mL FEU in a patient with low pre-test probability makes a diagnosis of DVT very unlikely. However, a D-dimer >=0.50 ug/mL FEU is nonspecific and may require additional diagnostic testing.

Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC):

Use reference interval of <0.50 ug/mL FEU. Narrative 01/05/2018 4:12 PM PST 63 year old woman with weight loss and abdominal pain. ** FINDINGS **: Technique:  Multiple contiguous axial CT images were obtained through the abdomen and pelvis following the administration of 106 mL of Omnipaque-300 intravenous contrast media. Positive oral contrast was not administered. Multiplanar reformats were obtained. CTDI: 6.31 mGy DLP: 278.41 mGy-cm Phantom: Body 32 Comparison: None CT Abdomen: Lung Base: Mild patchy consolidative and groundglass opacity at the extreme right lung base. Centrilobular emphysematous changes are noted at the lung bases. No pleural or pericardial effusion. Liver, Gallbladder, and Biliary System: The liver is normal in size and contour, without focal lesions. The gallbladder appears unremarkable. There is no intra-or extrahepatic biliary ductal dilatation. Spleen: The spleen is normal in size and no focal splenic lesions are seen. Pancreas: No concerning pancreatic lesions or pancreatic ductal dilatation are seen. Kidneys and Ureters: No concerning renal mass or hydronephrosis bilaterally. Some prominence of an extrarenal pelvis bilaterally, likely incidental. There there are multiple areas of left renal cortical thickening, likely chronic sequela of prior nonspecific insult. Adrenals: Unremarkable. Bowel: Overall, evaluation of bowel is limited by scant intra-abdominal fat. The stomach is decompressed and unremarkable. Abdominal small bowel loops are nondilated and without evidence for obstruction. The appendix is not identified in the right lower quadrant, no abnormal appendix is not seen. Intra-abdominal colon appears unremarkable. Lymph Nodes: Scattered mesenteric and retroperitoneal lymph nodes are identified, none of which appear pathologically enlarged. Vasculature: Atherosclerotic calcifications involve the abdominal aorta and branches. The aorta is of normal caliber. The portal venous system is patent. Peritoneum: No free fluid or free air. CT Pelvis: Bowel loops: Intrapelvic loop of small bowel appear unremarkable, without dilatation or wall thickening. The sigmoid colon and rectum appear unremarkable. A mild pericolonic edema of the descending and sigmoid colon is equivocal. Bladder: Unremarkable. Pelvic organs: Unremarkable. No free fluid is seen. Lymph Nodes: No pathologically enlarged pelvic lymph nodes are seen. Soft Tissues and Bones: No concerning abnormalities. History of Present Illness The patient, with a history of COPD and asthma, presents with persistent nausea, fatigue, and difficulty breathing. The patient reports feeling "winded" in the mornings and has been trying to walk around the block once or twice a day, but has been feeling unwell. The patient has been experiencing nausea for the past couple of weeks, initial symptoms started after Christmas which has been severe at times, and has been associated with a lack of appetite and a change in taste perception. The patient also reports having diarrhea, describing it as severe and frequent, and has been using Metamucil to manage it. The patient is a current smoker and is trying to quit, currently smoking about three cigarettes a day. The patient also uses marijuana, which she believes helps with her appetite. The patient is scheduled for a colonoscopy due to the ongoing diarrhea. She has also cut up alcohol intake which she states was exacerbating her symptoms. Patient has occasional nausea and a decrease in appetite. She denies abdominal pain, change in stool caliber, BRBPR, melena, vomiting, fever, night sweats, chills. They deny significant weight loss in the past 6-12 months. Patient has decreased tobacco smoking to 3 cigarettes daily. She smokes marijuana on occasion. She denies alcohol. Stools studies WNL as well as TTG. Anahit Petrosyan, MD ADULT/FAMILY MEDICINE 1011 RIVERSIDE AVENUE ROSEVILLE CA 95678-5134 SUBJECTIVE: Chief Complaint Patient presents with BRONCHITIS History of Present Illness Ms. Sharon, a patient with a history of COPD and emphysema, presents with worsening cough and chest congestion. She reports that her cough has been persistent but has worsened since last Friday. The cough is productive, with green sputum, and is associated with chest pain, particularly when she coughs. She also reports shortness of breath and has been using her inhalers, including a rescue inhaler, every four hours. She denies fever but reports feeling slightly warm. She also reports waking up with severe nausea and experiencing cold sweats, where her entire body becomes wet. She denies any recent sick contacts. She has a history of bronchitis, which she gets once a year, and she was given steroids last month for a similar episode. She also reports that she has been trying to quit smoking and has reduced her smoking to two cigarettes in one week. She has picked up smoking patches and plans to start using them. She also reports a history of nausea in the mornings, for which she was prescribed Zofran. You were treated by: Brainard, John Walter (M.D.) Your regular doctor is: AFSHAN UMAIR MD Follow Up: Surgery Department (925) 295-4110 Special Instructions: please follow up with your vascular surgeon Peripheral Artery Disease (PAD)  Peripheral artery disease (PAD) occurs when the arteries that carry blood to the arms and legs are narrowed or blocked. This is usually from a buildup of plaque. This is a fatty substance in the walls of the arteries. PAD most often affects the arteries in the legs. When these arteries are narrowed or blocked, less blood gets to the legs. This can cause leg and foot pain. If severe enough, the lack of blood flow can lead to tissue death (gangrene) and the loss of a toe, foot, or leg. Having PAD also makes it more likely that arteries in other body areas are blocked. For instance, arteries that carry blood to the heart or brain may be affected. This raises the chances of heart attack and stroke. Risk factors Certain things can make PAD more likely. They include: · Smoking · Diabetes · High blood pressure · Unhealthy cholesterol levels · Obesity · Inactive lifestyle · Older age · Family history of PAD Symptoms Many people with PAD have no symptoms. If symptoms do occur, they can include: · Pain in the muscles of the calves, thighs, or hips that gets worse with activity and better with rest (intermittent claudication) · Achy, tired, or heavy feeling in the legs · Weakness, numbness, tingling, or loss of feeling in the legs · If you smoke, quit. This helps prevent further damage to your arteries and lowers your health risks. Ask your provider about medicines or products that can help you quit smoking. Also consider joining a stop-smoking program or support group. · Be more active. This helps you lose weight and manage problems such as high blood pressure and unhealthy cholesterol levels. Start a walking program if advised to by your provider. Your provider may also help you form a safe exercise program that is right for your needs. · Make healthy eating changes. This includes eating less fat, salt, and sugar. · Take medicines for high blood pressure, unhealthy cholesterol levels, and diabetes as directed. · Have your blood pressure and cholesterol levels checked as often as directed. · If you have diabetes, try to keep your blood sugar well controlled. Test your blood sugar as directed. · If you are overweight, talk with your provider about a weight-loss plan. · Watch for cuts, scrapes, or open sores on your feet. Poor blood flow to the feet may slow healing and increase the risk for infection from these problems.  Follow-up care Follow up with your healthcare provider as advised. If you had imaging tests such as ultrasound, they will be reviewed by a doctor. You will be told the results and any new findings that may affect your care. When to seek medical advice  Call your healthcare provider right away if any of these occur: · Sudden severe pain in the legs or feet · Sudden cold, paleness, or blue color in the legs or feet · Weakness or numbness in the legs or feet that worsens · Any sore or wound in the legs or feet that won’t heal · Weak pulse in your legs or feet · Symptoms get worse or you have new symptoms Know the signs of heart attack and stroke People with PAD are at high risk for heart attack and stroke. Knowing the signs of these problems can help you protect your health and get help when you need it. Call 911 right away if you have any of the following: · Chest discomfort, such as pain, aching, tightness, or pressure that lasts more than a few minutes, or that comes and goes · Pain or discomfort in the arms, back, shoulders, neck, or jaw · Shortness of breath · Sweating (often a cold, clammy sweat) · Nausea · Lightheadedness · Sudden numbness, drooping, or weakness of the face, arms, or legs, especially on one side · Sudden confusion or trouble speaking or understanding · Sudden trouble seeing in one or both eyes · Sudden trouble walking, dizziness, or loss of balance · Sudden, severe headache with no known cause StayWell last reviewed this educational content on 11/1/2021 © 2000-2021 The StayWell Company, LLC. Discharge Instructions/Orders for Sharon F Crouch LOWER EXTREMITY ARTERIOGRAM AND INTERVENTION DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS for Sharon F Crouch Dr. Howard Young performed your ANGIOGRAM 8/23/2022. You underwent a procedure to evaluate the arterial circulation of your lower extremities with or without angioplasty/stenting to improve the circulation. ACTIVITY 1. Take it easy for 24 hours. 2. No vigorous physical activity or lifting for at least 3 days.

  1. Resume your regular diet as tolerated. WOUND CARE 1. Keep the plastic bandage on over the incision site for 24 hours. Keep the area clean and dry. 2. Remove plastic bandage after 24 hours. 3. DO NOT replace bandage with a new bandage. 4. Do not take a hot bath, hot tub or sauna until the site has healed. 5. You can shower after 24 hours. IF PROBLEMS ARISE: Call your physician if: 1. You start to bleed where the catheter was inserted. If you start to bleed, lie down flat and have a family member or friend apply continuous pressure on the bleeding area for 20 minutes and call 911 if it does not stop. 2. There is numbness, coolness or a change in color of the arm or leg where the at the puncture site. 3. Increasing swelling or discoloration in the treated limb or any toes/fingers. 4. You develop a fever as described below. 5. Any increasing pain or lump at the puncture site. Followup: If you have ongoing concerns related to your condition, please follow up with your primary care physician or physician who requested you come for today's procedure. Kaiser Walnut Creek Medical Center 1425 South Main Street Walnut Creek, CA 94596 Kaiser Antioch Medical Center 4501 Sand Creek Road Antioch, CA 94531 SHEILA SAHAR MOIN PA-C Resume your normal activities and diet. If you smoke, please stop. Smoking is harmful to your health. Please take all medications exactly as prescribed. These medicines are important to your health. Detailed information on how to take your medications is printed on your medication bottles. You should carry a list of current medications (prescriptions, and over the counter) and vitamins at all times. Keep this list up to date and share with your health care providers. It is especially important in emergency situations that caregivers know what medications you are taking. If prescription refills are required, please call your primary care physician or pharmacy. Make it a habit to call in your medication refills a week in advance. Note: controlled substances (i.e. narcotics) cannot be refilled without a new order from your physician. If you are concerned that you may be having a drug reaction, such as a rash, nausea, vomiting or diarrhea, please contact your primary care physician as soon as possible. If you have questions about your medications, please ask your nurse, caregiver, or a pharmacist. Narrative 08/23/2022 7:22 PM PDT 68 years old Female, smoker with recent onset of short distance right leg claudication ** TECHNIQUE **: PROCEDURE SUMMARY: - Arterial access with ultrasound guidance -Right lower extremity angiography as described below - Arterial interventions as described below - Post intervention Right lower extremity angiography Medications: Please see nursing record for sedation medications used. Other intraprocedural medications: None Radiation Dose -please see nursing records for radiation dose. Contrast: Please see nursing record for contrast dose. ** FINDINGS **: PROCEDURE DETAILS: Informed consent for the procedure including risks, benefits and alternatives was obtained and time-out was performed prior to the procedure.  The right-sided access site was prepared and draped using maximal sterile barrier technique including cutaneous antisepsis. Local analgesia was achieved with 2% lidocaine administered subcutaneously. The left common femoral artery was accessed with standard micropuncture technique and a sheath was placed.  Omniflush catheter was advanced into the distal abdominal aorta and pelvic angiogram was performed. Over angled glide wire, omniflush catheter was advanced into the right common femoral artery and the lower extremity runoff was performed to the right foot. Findings: Severe diffuse atheromatous changes are seen throughout the visualized arterial structures. Extensive calcifications are noted. The vessels as a whole are also quite gracile, especially of the iliac arteries bilaterally. Both internal iliac arteries are diseased but patent. The right common femoral artery is patent without significant stenosis. The right profunda is disease but is hypertrophied. There is diffuse disease in the SFA with short segment of occlusion in the abductor canal. There is a second longer occlusive segment at distal SFA and a third moderate to high-grade segmental stenosis at the junction of the distal SFA and popliteal arteries. There is two-vessel runoff in the leg with the peroneal artery being the dominant vessel. Anterior tibial is also patent. There is patency of the dorsal pedis as well as the distal posterior tibial artery plantar arteries are patent. Interventional procedure: A total of 6000 units of heparin were used for the procedure. In addition 400 mcg of intra-arterial nitroglycerin also were used. A 6 French destination sheath was advanced over wire so that the distal tip was within the lower right external iliac artery. An 0.035 advantage wire with crossing catheter was used to successfully traverse the occluded segments. Then, a 6 mm spider distal protection device was deployed in the distal popliteal artery. Then, a medium Hawk 1 directional atherectomy device was used to atherectomized all of the mentioned lesions. Approximately 4 passes were made in each segment. Then 5 mm chocolate balloon was used to dilate all of the affected segments. This was followed up with the use of 5 mm DCB over the treated segments. Follow-up arteriogram showed excellent angiographic results with complete patency of the SFA established. The spider distal protection device was retrieved. Post intervention: Right lower extremity runoff was performed to the foot. There is no evidence for embolic phenomena. Physical examination revealed a palpable right dorsal pedis artery, whereas prior to the procedure there was none. Vascular sheath was removed and hemostasis achieved with minx closure device. Complications: No immediate complications. ** HISTORY **: 68 years old Female, smoker with recent onset of short distance right leg claudication ** TECHNIQUE **: PROCEDURE SUMMARY: - Arterial access with ultrasound guidance -Right lower extremity angiography as described below - Arterial interventions as described below - Post intervention Right lower extremity angiography Medications: Please see nursing record for sedation medications used. Other intraprocedural medications: None Radiation Dose -please see nursing records for radiation dose. Vascular Surgery History and Physical Note Chief Complaint: CLAUDICATION History of Present Illness: Sharon F Crouch is a 68 Y female who presents for the evaluation of PVD. Notes right leg pain calf, shin, posterior thigh with walking that only started 2 months ago when in the hospital with COVID and UTI. Can barely walk a block although this varies. Also noted bluish discoloration of her toes started at that time. No issues with Left leg. Rest pain is not present. Ulceration is not present, but having tingling in right foot that is new two months ago. Trental / Cilostazole have not been tried. + smoker every day 3 cigs a day and will quit this weekend. PERIPHERAL VASCULAR DISEASE, UNSPECIFIED TYPE I73.9 68 Y female with asthma, HTN, lumbar spondylosis, hx od depression, cachexia, emphysema, current daily smoker, and PVD with new onset right leg pain and foot tingling started 2 months ago. Very short distance claudication. We had a lengthy discussion regarding leg pain with walking claudication symptoms and low risk of limb loss. However, given new onset of right foot tingling, cyanosis, short distance claudication and toe pressure of zero, we discussed right leg angiogram with intervention. Risks and benefits discussed. Angiogram was discussed with patient to improve perfusion to Right LE. Risks and benefits discussed such as risk including but not limited to bleeding, infection, clotting, embolization, need for additional procedures, unable to intervene on severe blockages, need for continued surveillance, need to be on antiplatelet medications if interventions are performed and the risk of renal injury with contrast. Medical management includes: - Aspirin or Plavix if unable to tolerate ASA - Statin therapy regardless of cholesterol panel - Good control of diabetes - Good control of blood pressure - Smoking cessation -she absolutely needs to stop smoking ASAP and before intervention and continue smoking cessation. We discussed risk of toe/limb loss with continued smoking. All questions were answered. I have confirmed the presence of the above clinical diagnoses, which were considered in the current and ongoing care of the patient. At the time of this visit, the medical record indicates, and/or the patient states, that there are no changes in these conditions unless otherwise noted. As treatment warrants, the patient has been advised to follow up with her PCP or appropriate specialist. Topics discussed as noted above. Janneth P.   • Stay at home except to get medical care.
  • Separate yourself from other people in your home. Do not have any visitors.
  • Wear a mask over your nose and mouth in indoor settings, including at home, especially if immuno-compromised or around those who are immunocompromised, unvaccinated, or at risk for severe disease.
  • Avoid sharing rooms/spaces with others; if not possible, open windows to outdoor air (if safe to do so) to improve ventilation or use portable air cleaners and exhaust fans.
  • Avoid using the same bathroom as others; if not possible, clean and disinfect after use.
  • Cover your coughs and sneezes.
  • Wash your hands often with soap and water for at least 20 seconds, or if you can't wash your hands, use an alcohol-based hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol.
  • Clean or disinfect "high-touch" surfaces.
  • Monitor your symptoms.
  • If you have symptoms or are sick, you should stay away from others even if they have some protection by having been previously infected in the past 3 months or by being fully vaccinated. Instructions for Caregivers/Family Members caring for you: -Caregivers/family Members who are vaccinated and received a booster or are not booster eligible do not need to quarantine and should monitor for symptoms.
